company shares.the_world_is: the world's listed company shares, one line per economy (world_listed_equity)
company shares.measured_as: the listed value, from that book, of each economy whose company shares have a pool on the ledger
company shares.why_this_quarter: the newest quarter at which no quarterly market in the listed-shares book is carried forward

debt securities.the_world_is: the world's bonds and bills at face value (world_debt_securities)

debt including loans.the_world_is: all debt of governments, companies and households in loans and securities (BIS total credit, all reporting countries) plus the bonds and bills of banks and other financial firms (world_debt_securities); government at market value where the BIS has it. The known part is the ledger's debt securities plus its loans, with loans held by securitisation vehicles taken out so no loan is counted twice

money.the_world_is: the world's broad money, economy by economy (world_money_usd); money is kept out of the ledger's total

source: Every figure is an owner line of one of the ownership books added up in the world ledger (Federal Reserve Financial Accounts, Bank of Japan Flow of Funds, ONS UK Economic Accounts, ECB and Eurostat quarterly sector accounts, Statistics Canada, the Central Bank of the Republic of China, India's exchange shareholding filings and the OECD financial balance sheets), converted with the International Monetary Fund's end-of-period exchange rates. The shares of the world come from the world listed-equity, debt-securities, total-credit and money books on this tab.
note: Each line is what one kind of owner holds across every pool of financial wealth the ledger can name - American company shares, Japanese government bonds, euro-area fund shares and the rest - so the lines add up to the ledger's total, and a line's share is that owner's slice of all the wealth this tab can account for. Where a country publishes its owners only as residents against foreigners, the residents stay on their own line rather than being guessed into households or funds, and what the publishers themselves could not place with an owner stays on a line of its own. Fund shares count twice, exactly as in the ledger: a fund is the owner of the shares and bonds it holds, and a household that owns units of the fund is the owner of those units; the checks say how much of the total that is. Loans held by mortgage pools and other securitisation vehicles count twice in the same way, once as the loan and once as the bond it backs, and the checks say how much that is too. The American owner lines, as the Federal Reserve publishes them, include the foreign shares and bonds Americans own; the ledger counts those in the country that issued them, so one line here takes them off once and the owners still add to the ledger's total. The checks also say how much of the world this covers: for company shares, the listed value of every economy whose shares are on the ledger, set against the world's listed shares at the newest quarter every quarterly market has reported, and for debt and money against the world's debt and money. Technical detail: each source book's owner lines are mapped to one kind of owner by their kind code (an unknown code stops the build), converted at the same International Monetary Fund end-of-quarter rate as the ledger, and carried forward by the ledger's rule, at most four quarters, using the owner lines of the date whose total is carried.
